Stem Cell Meat

By: Eugene Botha | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
........would you eat meat grown from stem cells?

Summary:
At the Univeristy of Maastricht scientists have begun producing meat from stem cells. They use a few stem cells and cultivate the few cells to grow into billions of cells in the lab and so produce edible meat that is indistinguishable from animal-grown meat.

Further information:
Lab-grown burgers 'will be on the menu by 2020': Scientists set up company to make stem cell meat an affordable reality
• Lab-grown burger from bovine stem cells could be on sale within 5 years

Whether or not we should continue to eat meat is an increasingly hot topic – its alleged impact on the climate and the ethical issues surrounding intensive farming have left many disillusioned with the carnivore's diet.
But scientists believe that they have a viable alternative that doesn’t involve sacrificing your steak for Quorn or lentils.
A Dutch team claim that their lab-grown burger made from bovine stem cells could be on sale within five years.

Appetising? The technology has already been proven on an individual scale. In 2013 scientists at Maastricht University, in the Netherlands cooked and ate the first lab-grown hamburger
They have even set up a company in a bid to make the burger taste better and cheaper to produce.
In 2013, the team cooked and ate a burger that cost £215,000 to produce.
A 142g 'cultured beef' patty, developed at Maastricht University, was lightly fried in a little butter and sunflower oil and took three months to grow in a laboratory, using cells from a living cow.
The burgers are created in a four-step process. First, stem cells — which have the power to turn into any other cell — are stripped from cow muscle, which is taken during a harmless biopsy.
Next, the cells are incubated in a nutrient ‘broth’ until they multiply many times over, creating a sticky tissue.
This is then bulked up through the laboratory equivalent of exercise — it is anchored to Velcro and stretched.
Finally, 20,000 strips of the meat are minced and mixed with salt, breadcrumbs, egg powder and natural red colourants to form an edible patty.
The head of the new firm, Peter Verstrate, said in an interview with the BBC: ‘I feel extremely excited about the prospect of this product being on sale.
'I am confident that we will have it on the market in five years,' he said.
He went on to explain that the 'meat' would initially only be available as an exclusive product but would be on supermarket shelves once a demand and reasonable price had been established.
It has just been revealed that Sergey Brin is one of the financial backers of the test-tube burger.
Mr Brin is an American computer scientist and Internet entrepreneur who, with Larry Page, co-founded Google.
Together with Page, he owns 16 per cent of the internet search giant.
His personal wealth is estimated to be £13.2bn in 2012.
He and Page previously invested in a large offshore wind farm in 2010 and a self-driving car in a bid to reduce road accidents via Google's philanthropic arm.
It is believed that Mr Brin invested £215,000 in the creation of the burger.
Mr Brin has also invested in Space Adventures - the private space tourism company that is selling £65 million trips to the Moon.
He has also previously worked with film director James Cameron to investigate mining asteroids and has an interest in solving the world’s energy and climate problems.
His technique, he says, can be used to recreate the flesh of most animals, including rare species such as tigers or pandas, although demand may be questionable.
The initial project was backed by Google co-founder Sergey brin.
At the time of the 2013 demonstration he said he was confident that man-made meat would do a great deal to help humanity.
In a video message played to attendees, he said: 'Sometimes when technology comes along, it has the capability to transform how we view our world.
'I like to look at technology opportunities. When technology seems like it is on the cusp of viability and if it succeeds there, it can be really transformative for the world.'
'There are basically three things that can happen going forward - one is that we can all become vegetarian. I don't think that's really likely.
'The second is we ignore the issues and that leads to continued environmental harm and the third option is we do something new.
'Some people think this is science fiction - it's not real, it's somewhere out there. I actually think that's a good thing.'

Press Release:


Meat the Future
Fancy a juicy, tender cut of laboratory-reared meat? Scientists at the Dutch University of Maastricht have begun producing meat indistinguishable from the animal-grown variety in a lab since 2013. Back then they cooked and ate a 142g patty that cost £215,000 to produce over three months, using cells from a living cow. Carte Blanche asks whether science could simultaneously solve the problem of rising global appetites for meat and the devastating toll of farm-derived meat production on the environment?


Script:


Mark Post:
Yes, of course I have tasted my own hamburger and as you can see I am still alive.
V/O:
Mark Post is Professor of Vascular Physiology at the University of Maastricht in the Netherlands. The hamburger he is referring to is this one. And although it looks quite ordinary, it is far from it. In fact, some people actually find it ghastly.
Derek link:
What makes Mark’s hamburger so controversial is the fact that the meat it consists of was never part of a living animal. It was grown in its entirety in a laboratory.
V/O:
This sounds like something straight from the pages of a science fiction novel, but it is in fact a reality.

As Vascular Specialist Mark has extensive experience with tissue engineering. He has been growing blood vessels in the lab for many years.
Mark:
We are using tissue engineering which basically means using stem cells making arteries for bypass grafting. For people who need bypasses and don’t have their own blood vessels to provide that.
Derek link
While Mark and his team were working on growing blood vessels for transplants, they also started thinking out of the box.
Mark:
I thought, well if you do the same things with skeletal muscle you might be able to produce beef, or any other type of meat. So we got intrigued by that idea and started to tissue engineer skeletal muscle.
V/O:
The meat we eat every day is nothing but skeletal muscle tissue. The idea of alternative meat production was also appealing to Mark because he knew that cattle farming had become more and more controversial over time.
Mark:
Meat production is actually a very problematic thing. First of all it requires a lot of resources. It requires a lot of food for the animals and a lot of land. About 70% of all our edible land is used to feed animals instead of directly feeding people.
V/O:
Economist Dawie Roodt agrees that livestock farming is problematic because of the impact on the environment.
Dawie:
A number of concerns environmentally. One is of course is that they use a lot of water. Water is a very scarce resource. Another concern is that they are using space. Space that we could have used for something else, for recreation or a game park as an example. And also keep in mind that we have a lot of sheep and cattle out there. We have literally billions of them out there. And billions of cattle and billions of cows can fart quite a lot.
V/O:
And when farting, cattle and sheep produce methane, a very powerful greenhouse gas. Much more potent than CO2. In fact, the 1 and half billion cattle and 1 point 9 billion sheep contribute between 15 and 20 percent of the world’s greenhouse gasses.
Derek:
Is the demand for red meat actually increasing globally?
Dawie:
Well the demand for red meat is increasing without a doubt. People are getting wealthier. And as people get wealthier they eat more carbohydrates and then eventually they start eating more protein as well. They initially start off with cheaper protein for example chicken or fish. And eventual they move over to more expensive protein like for example beef and the like.
Derek:
And in countries like China and India the appetite for red meat is seems is growing?
Dawie:
China is a very interesting example because the Chinese economy and the Chinese society is actually morphing into a different kind of society. They used to be a production society up till now and now they are becoming a consumer society. They have become wealthier and as you become wealthy you want a flat, go on overseas holiday, have a car, and you want a nice piece of beef.
V/O:
Beef consumption in India is also rapidly increasing which means that worldwide beef will become very scarce and expensive in the near future.
Derek link:
Another reason why it makes sense to look for alternative ways to produce meat is the question of animal welfare.
Mark:
I think we all know that the very intense livestock industry comes with animal welfare issues. I also think that we became increasingly more uncomfortable with that idea. So that will be another benefit of using this technology to produce meat.
V/O:
So there are really compelling reasons to explore alternative ways to produce meat.

But exactly how does it work?
Mark:
We all have, and cows and every vertebrate animal, has stem cells in their muscle. They’re just sitting there waiting to repair in case of injury. So if we have a tear in our muscle its repaired by muscle tissue, but these stem cells. So they can do that because they can proliferate and they can form the tissue again. They can do that inside of the body but they can also do that outside of the body if you provide the right conditions.
V/O:
Muscle stem cells are harvested in a harmless procedure from a living animal.

The cells are then deposited into a growth medium. The stacks are then placed in an incubator where the cells start to divide and proliferate rapidly.
Mark:
And their proliferation capacity is tremendous. From a couple of cells you can produce thousands of thousands of kilos of beef.
V/O:
Once there are enough cells they are moved to trays with central tubular scaffolds.
Mark:
If you create a temporary tissue structure for them so that they know in which form they need to align, and you create anchor point. Because muscle need anchor points to hold onto. Then they will start to form a tissue in and by itself.
V/O:
The stem cells grow into small rings of muscle tissue that are then harvested. The rings are cut and form small strips of tissue. These strips are the basis of the lab grown meat.
Mark:
So for ground beef that is fine. Then you put these small little tissues together with breadcrumbs and egg white and what else is being used to make a hamburger.
V/O:
The muscle tissue is whitish because it contains no blood or globin. Some beetroot juice is added to give it colour.
Derek Link:
Two years ago Mark used 10 000 pieces of their lab grown meat to create the world’s first in-vitro hamburger.
V/O:
The reveal of the first stem cell burger was big event and covered by the world media. It was calculated that this burger cost in the region of three million rand to produce. A panel of food experts was assembled to taste the burger in a television studio.
Mark:
The first burger we produced in 2013 only had muscle tissue. Nothing else. The tasters who commented on it on live television said “Yeah you know its meat but its kind of dry” And that’s because it didn’t have any fat tissue in it.
V/O:
Since that first burger made headlines the scientists at Maastricht University have come a long way. To counter the dryness of the meat they have also started to grow fat from stem cells to combine with the meat in order to enhance the taste.
Derek:
So far Mark and his team have been able to produce hamburger meat in the lab. But what about meat lovers with a craving for a prime steak?
Mark:
For large tissues, for a steak, it’s more complex. And that’s the same issue with tissue engineering for medical purposes. Once you need a thicker piece of tissue or a larger piece of tissue you would need a channel system or a blood vessel system to get all the oxygen and nutrients in all nooks and crannies of the tissue. Otherwise the centre will just die.
V/O:
They are working on this challenge at the moment, and Mark is confident that they will soon be able to produce steak as well.
Derek link:
Many people have a negative reaction when they first hear of meat grown from stem cells, but Mark says his lab in-vitro meat is actually safer.
Mark:
This is absolutely safe. You know it’s not a weird kind of product. It’s actually exactly the same tissue that we are used to eating.
V/O:
The only difference is that you can be absolutely sure that there are no pesticides, antibiotics or hormones in the stem cell beef.

Mark is upbeat about the future of cultured meat.
Mark:
For the larger public to accept this, it needs to be cheap and it need to be tasty. Those are the most important parts in food.
V/O:
By adding fat they have made the meat much tastier. The next big priority is to find a way to reduce the production costs.

Last year a dedicated company was founded to upscale and commercialize stem cell meat. And this will soon start to bring down the price enormously, making it very affordable.
Derek Link:
Mark calculates that if they upscale their operation they would within 5 years be able to bring down the production cost of the stem cell meat to around 2 Euros a kilo – that is between R30 and R40.
V/O:
And the process also works for other types of animal protein such a fish and chicken.
Mark:
Because all these animals have these stem cells sitting in their muscle tissue.
Derek:
Now do you really think this is an alternative to traditional cattle farming?
Dawie:
Well without a doubt I think technology is one of those obvious things that’s going to change the way that we look at the world. Change the way that we live. Change the way that we consume certain things. Why not take the next obvious step and make use of technology to make other kinds of food?
Derek:
The crunch question literally Dawie: Would you eat a hamburger grown from stem cells?
Dawie:
Well is you give me a hamburger grown from stem cells with some nice chips and a nice beer! Without a doubt!

And this will soon start to bring down the price enormously, making it very affordable. Derek Link: Mark calculates that if they upscale their operation they would within 5 years be able to bring down the production cost of the stem cell meat to around 2 Euros a kilo – that is between R30 and R40. V/O: And the process also works for other types of animal protein such a fish and chicken. Mark: Because all these animals have these stem cells sitting in their muscle tissue. Derek: Now do you really think this is an alternative to traditional cattle farming? Dawie: Well without a doubt I think technology is one of those obvious things that’s going to change the way that we look at the world. Change the way that we live. Change the way that we consume certain things. Why not take the next obvious step and make use of technology to make other kinds of food? Derek: The crunch question literally Dawie: Would you eat a hamburger grown from stem cells? Dawie: Well is you give me a hamburger grown from stem cells with some nice chips and a nice beer! metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): ........would you eat meat grown from stem cells?
metadata.Summary: At the Univeristy of Maastricht scientists have begun producing meat from stem cells. They use a few stem cells and cultivate the few cells to grow into billions of cells in the lab and so produce edible meat that is indistinguishable from animal-grown meat.
metadata.Further information: Lab-grown burgers 'will be on the menu by 2020': Scientists set up company to make stem cell meat an affordable reality • Lab-grown burger from bovine stem cells could be on sale within 5 years Whether or not we should continue to eat meat is an increasingly hot topic – its alleged impact on the climate and the ethical issues surrounding intensive farming have left many disillusioned with the carnivore's diet. But scientists believe that they have a viable alternative that doesn’t involve sacrificing your steak for Quorn or lentils. A Dutch team claim that their lab-grown burger made from bovine stem cells could be on sale within five years. Appetising? The technology has already been proven on an individual scale. In 2013 scientists at Maastricht University, in the Netherlands cooked and ate the first lab-grown hamburger They have even set up a company in a bid to make the burger taste better and cheaper to produce. In 2013, the team cooked and ate a burger that cost £215,000 to produce. A 142g 'cultured beef' patty, developed at Maastricht University, was lightly fried in a little butter and sunflower oil and took three months to grow in a laboratory, using cells from a living cow. The burgers are created in a four-step process. First, stem cells — which have the power to turn into any other cell — are stripped from cow muscle, which is taken during a harmless biopsy. Next, the cells are incubated in a nutrient ‘broth’ until they multiply many times over, creating a sticky tissue. This is then bulked up through the laboratory equivalent of exercise — it is anchored to Velcro and stretched. Finally, 20,000 strips of the meat are minced and mixed with salt, breadcrumbs, egg powder and natural red colourants to form an edible patty. The head of the new firm, Peter Verstrate, said in an interview with the BBC: ‘I feel extremely excited about the prospect of this product being on sale. 'I am confident that we will have it on the market in five years,' he said. He went on to explain that the 'meat' would initially only be available as an exclusive product but would be on supermarket shelves once a demand and reasonable price had been established. It has just been revealed that Sergey Brin is one of the financial backers of the test-tube burger. Mr Brin is an American computer scientist and Internet entrepreneur who, with Larry Page, co-founded Google. Together with Page, he owns 16 per cent of the internet search giant. His personal wealth is estimated to be £13.2bn in 2012. He and Page previously invested in a large offshore wind farm in 2010 and a self-driving car in a bid to reduce road accidents via Google's philanthropic arm. It is believed that Mr Brin invested £215,000 in the creation of the burger. Mr Brin has also invested in Space Adventures - the private space tourism company that is selling £65 million trips to the Moon. He has also previously worked with film director James Cameron to investigate mining asteroids and has an interest in solving the world’s energy and climate problems. His technique, he says, can be used to recreate the flesh of most animals, including rare species such as tigers or pandas, although demand may be questionable. The initial project was backed by Google co-founder Sergey brin. At the time of the 2013 demonstration he said he was confident that man-made meat would do a great deal to help humanity. In a video message played to attendees, he said: 'Sometimes when technology comes along, it has the capability to transform how we view our world. 'I like to look at technology opportunities. When technology seems like it is on the cusp of viability and if it succeeds there, it can be really transformative for the world.' 'There are basically three things that can happen going forward - one is that we can all become vegetarian. I don't think that's really likely. 'The second is we ignore the issues and that leads to continued environmental harm and the third option is we do something new. 'Some people think this is science fiction - it's not real, it's somewhere out there. I actually think that's a good thing.'
